entries.title: ‘Society Gumbo’
entries.summary: In 1951 the San Francisco Chronicle wrote that “in Sausalito people live on anything that floats.” Those midcentury houseboat dwellers were the antecedents of Marin County’s “anchor-outs,” people who live on the anchorage in Richardson Bay and therefore, as Piper French writes in her review of Joe Kloc’s Lost at Sea in our September 24 […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In 1951 the San Francisco Chronicle wrote that “in Sausalito people live on anything that floats.” Those midcentury houseboat dwellers were the antecedents of Marin County’s “anchor-outs,” people who live on the anchorage in Richardson Bay and therefore, as Piper French writes in her review of Joe Kloc’s Lost at Sea in our September 24 issue, “outside the bounds of mainstream American life.” According to the county authorities and neighbors on dry land, the anchor-outs are also homeless, and their not-always-seaworthy vessels are a threat to the bay’s ecosystem. (“Locals are positively racked by anxiety over the fate of the bay’s eelgrass,” French writes.) “They spar with the harbormaster…weather storms and the pandemic, [and] get displaced to dry land,” but, as French points out, “Sausalito’s extreme shortage of truly affordable housing, and its unwillingness to construct any sort of shelter, means that the anchor-outs have little hope of staying in the county” if they leave their houseboats. “Whether we admit it to ourselves or not,” exile and disappearance are “the intended result of our standard approach to homelessness.”

Before relocating to New York City, French lived for five years in Los Angeles, where she reported on California politics and the criminal legal system. Her writing on housing, migration, state violence, and the death penalty has appeared in a range of publications, including The New Republic, New York, and The Drift. For the NYR Online, she has written about, among other subjects, the Global Sumud Flotilla, the relationship between labor unions and migrant workers in Los Angeles, and Trump’s family separation policies.

I emailed French this summer to ask her about the antigrowth movement, Proposition 13, hippies, and making a living in long-form journalism.

Maggie McGowan: Marin County classifies the “anchor-outs” as homeless. It seems safe to say that that classification best serves the people who live on land and who want the anchor-outs to go elsewhere. Many of the anchor-outs Joe Kloc meets would not describe themselves that way. Is there an alternative to “homeless” or “unhoused” that could better represent their situation, perhaps to their advantage?

Piper French: This isn’t a municipal categorization, but I’m partial to the painter Jean Varda’s take on the hippies who lived on houseboats in Sausalito in the 1960s—the proto-anchor-outs. In his cousin Agnès Varda’s short film Uncle Yanco, which I discuss in the piece, Jean says his neighbors are “not the sort of rebels who carry pistols—they are rebels against the system, against this American obsession with making money.” I think there is something constitutionally rebellious about the way the anchor-outs live, or lived. They refuse to abide by bourgeois values; they’re renegades who live by a unique code and participate in a sharing economy (not unlike the veteran ravers in Oliver Laxe’s recent film Sirāt—though it doesn’t go too well for them, either). During happier days, they described their community as a “society gumbo,” but they also call it the “washing machine” and the “war zone.” Some of these descriptions are a bit inscrutable, but they’re all more meaningful than “homeless.”

The Sausalito “Hill People”—those lucky enough to afford houses on land—frequently cite environmental concerns to justify evicting the anchor-outs. As you write, these concerns may not always be in good faith. But as climate change displaces more and more people—as it did after the 2025 LA wildfires—a balance between a (genuine) environmentalism and an effective approach to the housing crisis seems only more urgent. What do you think such a balance might look like?

I don’t doubt that Marinites are genuinely concerned about their natural environment. But the focus on the anchor-outs’ relatively modest contribution to bay pollution is indicative of a broader tendency, by no means unique to Marin County, to blame homeless people for everything that goes wrong. A few years back in LA, for instance, the county governing body voted to ban the unhoused from certain high-fire areas, arguing that they were contributing to brush fires. Of course there is a fire risk associated with sleeping rough, but most encampment fires start in dense neighborhoods like Skid Row. It’s arguably a much bigger problem that wealthy homeowners build homes in the remotest reaches of the Santa Monica mountains, on land that is fated to burn, and burns more fiercely the more you try to stifle it—and then keep rebuilding even when those homes fall prey to the next wildfire.

This isn’t entirely the fault of the very rich, either: California’s ever-sprawling population has spurred new suburban development in rural areas that are especially fire prone. The state legislature has tried to solve this conundrum by allowing greater density in urban zones, but these bills tend to require that only a small percentage of new, high-density housing be truly affordable, which will not alleviate the housing crisis. Regardless, the dangers of living in the foothills have been illustrated in horrifying fashion by the wholesale destruction of Altadena and the Palisades; those fires were an environmental disaster whose fallout we’ll be reckoning with for decades to come—and the outrageous price gouging and opportunistic land grabs that occurred in the aftermath certainly show that cities need firmer regulations in place to prevent this sort of vulture capitalism.

You wrote about Marin County for the NYR Online three years ago, when locals, citing environmental concerns, opposed a development that was designed, at least in part, to respond to Marin’s housing crisis. In that essay you argue that “the crisis is not, of course, unique to Marin, but it’s particularly palpable on the soil from which the first seeds of the antigrowth movement sprouted.” What about Marin County made it such fertile soil for the antigrowth movement? Is Marin’s hostility toward the anchor-outs an offshoot of this movement?

Anyone who’s had the pleasure of spending time in Marin knows how beautiful it is—there’s a reason people always reach for celestial metaphors. After the construction of the Golden Gate Bridge, it was also as little as fifteen minutes from the heart of a world-class city. Unsurprisingly, there was a massive population explosion in the postwar era, and that led to the start of the antigrowth movement.

It has always seemed a little ironic to me that amid this bastion of natural preservation, you have this massive prison complex, San Quentin, sitting atop some of California’s most valuable “waterfront property.” When I first heard about the proposal to convert a parcel of the prison land into an affordable housing complex, to take advantage of the fact that state land is exempt from certain requirements that often serve to throw sand in the gears of new development, it seemed like a perfect nexus of phenomena from which to explore land use battles in the state. The insanely high valuation of most land in Marin County and locals’ reluctance to countenance new development have led to these acrobatic maneuvers—converting a former gun range where prison guards would do target practice into apartment buildings for teachers! At the same time, Marin’s reputation as an affluent and lily-white enclave leads people to interpret any resistance to new development as classic NIMBYism—even though another case I looked at where locals opposed new housing, in historically black Marin City, arguably had more to do with fear about gentrification and displacement.

That being said, I don’t think the hostility toward the anchor-outs is something unique to Marin. If anything, they were perhaps afforded slightly more tolerance because they were seen as a curio.

One of the anchor-outs tells Kloc that many of Sausalito’s landlubber residents were once part of “the Haight-Ashbury scene, the Summer of Love scene, the houseboat scene,” but in the Eighties and Nineties they moved on, “first financially and then ideologically.” The ex-hippie-turned-square-turned-Reagan-voter is a fairly familiar trope, probably one without much explanatory power. But it is striking that California homeowners’ “tax revolt” began just a few years after the Summer of Love. (It’s striking, too, that the anchor-out tells Kloc, “Every Judas has been a real estate agent.”) Is there any connection between the two?

I love the Judas line. My guess is that the anchor-outs, or at least some of them, see real estate agents’ commodification of the land as a betrayal of the values of California’s earlier inhabitants and contrary to their whole ethos. (Their decision to opt out by living on the water instead is bedeviling to authorities in part because it seems like they’re getting away with something.)

I think there are both material and cultural reasons for the shift you describe. The tax revolt was a successful attempt by a small group of ideologues to capitalize on people’s justifiable anger at the cost-of-living crisis that followed the war in Vietnam, along with California’s runaway home prices. One hugely consequential victory of this movement was 1978’s Proposition 13, a public subsidy for homeowners that increases the longer you stay put (it dialed back home value assessments to 1975 values, and limited tax increases to one percent of that assessed value, plus inflation, going forward, seriously hollowing out the state’s tax base). Californians are still living in the society Proposition 13 made: the state used to have some of the best-resourced public schools in the country, and now it doesn’t.

I think Marin’s trajectory perfectly encapsulates some of the foreclosed possibilities of the 1960s. The astonishing social movements of the decade—particularly the black freedom struggle and the antiwar movement—could have produced a more durable sense of solidarity and collective possibilities. But there was very real and concentrated state repression against the more militant aspects and members of these movements. In fact, in 1972 Angela Davis was tried for allegedly participating in an effort to free the imprisoned black radical writer George Jackson at the Marin County Superior Court.

On the other hand, a lot of hippies turned inward, toward spiritualism and self-improvement. This can all veer very quickly into kooky right-wing territory, as we’ve seen with the MAHA movement more recently, which definitely has its hooks deep into the moms of Marin County. In the essay, I recommend Emmett Grogan’s book Ringolevio because—for all his fabulism—Grogan is quite clear-eyed about the narcissism and self-interest of the hippies. The passage about the group of hippies going out to the pueblo and giving the Native kids LSD and hooking up on the tribe’s sacred ground until they get run off is priceless. Reading Ringolevio gave me a better appreciation for how that shift into the 1980s transpired—and how it perhaps wasn’t such a stretch as it might appear. People looking back at the 1960s tend to assume everyone was sort of equally aligned against the system, but alongside the committed student and black and antiwar radicals, there were always a lot of people who just wanted to get high and listen to good music (forgivable!).The counterculture became the culture—and by the 1980s the thing to do was make piles of money off the stock market. (We saw this again in 2020 and beyond—how resolutely people took up the mantle of protest against the police, and then how casually most of those who aren’t personally affected by abusive policing have shrugged it off again.)

Your essay concludes with a reflection on the financial difficulties that come with working in print journalism. Do you have any advice to young writers? How do you navigate the steadily shrinking world of long-form journalism?

I hesitate to give generalized advice because the industry has contracted substantially just in the few years I’ve been in it, and I don’t think it’s a matter of following the right steps anymore, if it ever was. I would, however, strongly suggest spending time doing other sorts of work. The piecemeal and in some cases very bad jobs that I had throughout my twenties—waiting tables, bartending, canvassing, working with asylum seekers and farmworkers, contact tracing during the pandemic—have greatly informed my writing and reporting. They have also made me appreciate it more. Long-form journalism is absurdly labor-intensive, it can be personally demoralizing, and there’s even something depressing about succeeding to whatever meager extent in an industry that’s collapsing around you. I carry my memories of the work I did before as a reminder that it’s a gift to get to spend my days reading widely, talking to interesting people from all sorts of backgrounds, and trying to make sense of the world.

I do think cultivating close editorial relationships is one of the most important things you can do as a young writer. That sort of community is essential when you’re independent, and it’s helpful to be able to frankly discuss money and how people are making it—or not. (Recently The Baffler ran a forum on writers and their side hustles; on the Substack “How I Make Money Writing,” writers talk openly about their finances to help demystify the economics of media work.) I do also recommend not living in New York. I live here at the moment, but I’m glad I didn’t move here right after college, and I don’t think it’s the only place in the world to be. Finally, there’s really no way around it: you have to get good at living without spending too much and ideally figure out how to go about making your life rich in nonmonetary ways. It can be done!

entries.title: An Exception in World Affairs
entries.summary: Ratko Mladić’s death last week at eighty-three in The Hague—where he was serving a life sentence for committing war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide as the commander of the Bosnian Serb forces during the war in Bosnia from 1992 to 1995—is a reminder that the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was the […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Ratko Mladić’s death last week at eighty-three in The Hague—where he was serving a life sentence for committing war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide as the commander of the Bosnian Serb forces during the war in Bosnia from 1992 to 1995—is a reminder that the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was the most effective instrument the international community has devised since the tribunal at Nuremberg to hold accountable those responsible for great crimes. Indeed, in certain respects it went beyond the precedent that Nuremberg set. Where that tribunal had brought to justice only defendants from a defeated nation, the ICTY tried, convicted, and sentenced perpetrators from all parties to the conflicts that took place across the former Yugoslavia between 1991 and 1999.

When the war in Bosnia began in April 1992, I was the director of Human Rights Watch. In late July, HRW released a book-length report documenting the crimes committed in the first four months of the conflict. We also proposed the creation of an international tribunal—the first time we had sought the establishment of such a body. Two factors made Bosnia different from previous conflicts we had monitored. The first was that it involved three states: Bosnia, Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (then consisting of Serbia and Montenegro). Other conflicts we had documented took place within a single country and were considered internal in nature. Under international law at that time, the concept of war crimes only applied to international armed conflicts. The second factor was the similarity between the crimes being committed by Bosnian Serb forces and those of the Nazis during World War II. Serb forces had coined the term “ethnic cleansing” to describe their displacement of Bosnian Muslims and of Croats, and had established several camps in Bosnia that evoked comparisons to Buchenwald and Dachau. A tribunal similar to that at Nuremberg seemed an appropriate response.

Our report appeared at a moment when the mainstream press had just discovered the torture, rape, and other gross abuses being committed by Bosnian Serb forces in camps such as Omarska and Keraterm, and so the proposal for a tribunal caught on quickly. Yet when the ICTY was established by the United Nations Security Council, it was derided by many. István Deák, a prominent historian of central and eastern Europe, wrote in the pages of this magazine that while “the Nuremberg court was created after the enemy had been defeated in a total war lasting almost six years,” the ICTY “is being set up without the slightest intention of defeating and apprehending the criminals.” He also criticized the UN for simultaneously working with the new Serbian president, Slobodan Milošević, “a primary candidate for indictment in the proposed war crimes trial,” to secure a peace agreement in Bosnia, arguing that “the entire affair of a tribunal smacks of cynicism and hypocrisy.” When I wrote a lengthy letter to the editors defending the effort, Deák reiterated that he believed states might “use the international tribunal as a face-saving measure and a substitute for action.”

Several years later I got a letter from Deák, who died at the age of ninety-six in 2023, saying that he had been mistaken. The tribunal, he acknowledged, had proved its value. I responded, confessing that when we debated I was not yet sure how the ICTY would develop. But I thought that only by defending it could I give it a chance to fulfill my hopes.

In the years that followed, the successes of the ICTY—and the somewhat more limited achievements of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda that it inspired—helped lead to the creation of the International Criminal Court, which began operating in 2002. That body was envisioned as a global and permanent version of the ICTY and the ICTR, a court that could hold the most terrible of criminals to account for the gravest of crimes. It is still finding its way: it began with what some thought was a disproportionate focus on Africa, and has had difficulty gaining custody of defendants.

Yet today the United States is engaged in a campaign to destroy the ICC, seemingly motivated, as I have previously written in these pages, by the desire to absolve the US’s ally Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu—who is now running for reelection—for Israel’s crimes in Gaza. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on personnel of the court, which it has called “corrupt and fatally politicized.” All of this raises the alarming possibility that Mladić’s present-day counterparts, of which there are a number, may not have to fear that they will suffer his fate.

The ICTY faced considerable hurdles, both in its creation and in carrying out its mission. By October 1992 the UN Security Council had established a commission to collect evidence of war crimes. But President George H. W. Bush was reluctant to speak out on international affairs while running for reelection against Bill Clinton, who made the economy his focus (“it’s the economy, stupid”). Only after Bush’s defeat did Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger—a former ambassador to Yugoslavia who was sometimes known as “Lawrence of Yugoslavia”—endorse the establishment of a tribunal. Clinton’s designated ambassador to the UN, Madeleine Albright, then devoted herself to the body’s creation; she liked to be known as “the mother of the tribunal.”

Advertisement

After the Security Council voted in May 1993 to establish the ICTY, a battle ensued over who would serve as its chief prosecutor. Some nominees were rightly rejected because they were not qualified, but others were vetoed for political reasons. Russia blocked any nominee from a NATO country. An outstanding jurist, Soli Sorabjee, who had served as India’s attorney general, was blocked by Pakistan, then a member of the Security Council. At long last, in July 1994, the council approved another very fine lawyer, Richard Goldstone of South Africa. A strong opponent of apartheid, he had been appointed to his country’s Constitutional Court by Nelson Mandela, who agreed to grant him a two-year leave from that post so he could join the ICTY. Russia, which was protective of the Serbs, did not impede the appointment because it wanted to be on good terms with Mandela.

When Goldstone began at the tribunal, there was only one low-level detainee in custody, a former guard at one of the camps. The prosecutors who had been hired before Goldstone’s appointment were busy pursuing indictments against other low-ranking figures, approaching their task as if they were building a case against an organized crime syndicate, in which plea bargains would be used to get foot soldiers to testify against the bosses. They did not seem to understand that the tribunal needed to show that it could take on those with the highest level of responsibility for the most serious crimes. It took Goldstone time to reorient the prosecution, but by July 1995 he had indicted Radovan Karadžić, the Bosnian Serb political leader, and Ratko Mladić, the military leader.

Karadžić and Mladić were charged for such crimes as the shelling and sniping from the hills surrounding Sarajevo that killed about 10,000 civilians and injured many thousands more. I still vividly recall what it was like to move about that besieged city, which I visited several times during the war, always trying to stay out of the line of fire by making sure that I did not cross streets at places that could be seen from the hills. At the Holiday Inn where I stayed, I only took rooms without a view. (I was grateful that the US ambassador lent me his bulletproof car for one trip to the airport, which was controlled by UN forces. Another time, I made that trip inside an armored personnel carrier.)

Unbeknownst to Goldstone, around the time he obtained the indictments of Karadžić and Mladić, Bosnian Serb forces executed roughly eight thousand Muslim men and boys captured from the town of Srebrenica. The massacre was discovered some weeks after it took place, exposed by a journalist for The Christian Science Monitor, David Rohde, and by satellite photos that the US government made public. Goldstone responded by indicting Karadžić and Mladić again for these additional crimes. The two sets of indictments made it impossible for them to travel to Dayton, Ohio, in November 1995 to take part in negotiations to end the war in Bosnia. The Bosnian Serbs empowered Milošević to represent their interests at Dayton, and it was he who signed the peace agreement. (Milošević himself was subsequently indicted for crimes committed during the war in Kosovo, but died before his trial was completed.)

Under the Dayton agreement, about 60,000 NATO troops were deployed to Bosnia to enforce the peace. Although these troops were furnished with photos of the accused war criminals indicted by the ICTY, they did not make arrests even when they encountered them, apparently fearing retaliation from Serbs. All this began to change after Tony Blair became prime minister of the United Kingdom in 1997 and appointed Robin Cook as foreign secretary. Cook was intent on cooperating with the ICTY, and under his direction British troops in Bosnia started making arrests. When the British forces suffered no retaliation, American troops and those from some other countries began to follow suit. Over time the ICTY was able to obtain custody of all 161 surviving indictees, many of whom were handed over by the governments of the countries of the former Yugoslavia under strong pressure from the European Union.

Advertisement

Karadžić and Mladić were among the last to be taken into custody. Karadžić was captured in Serbia in 2008. Trained as a psychiatrist before he entered politics, he had been living in the Belgrade area under an assumed name since the end of the war, heavily disguised and apparently earning a living as a practitioner of alternative medicine. Now eighty-one, he is serving his life sentence in a British prison.

Mladić was not captured until 2011. He, too, had been hiding under a different name, but otherwise had lived openly at the home of a family member in northern Serbia. On at least a couple of occasions he took part in activities that must have attracted public attention, as when he attended a football match in Belgrade. Perhaps he felt safe in the knowledge that many of his fellow Serbs regarded him as a hero for his military exploits. It seems likely, however, that the Serbian government facilitated his arrest, which was an essential condition of the country eventually securing EU membership. When he was arrested he offered no resistance, perhaps recognizing that his capture was inevitable.

Many human rights advocates hoped that the ICTY’s performance would inaugurate a new era for international justice, in which the world would understand that the kinds of abuses that took place during the wars in the former Yugoslavia would be punished—and in which they would therefore, ultimately, be deterred. There have been some successes. For example, the west African countries of Liberia and Sierra Leone benefitted greatly from a Special Court for Sierra Leone—established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leonean government—which, among other things, convicted former Liberian dictator Charles Taylor in 2012 for his many crimes. He is currently serving out his fifty-year sentence in the United Kingdom.

This fall the former president of the Philippines, Rodrigo Duterte, will go on trial at the International Criminal Court for the extrajudicial killings of many thousands of suspected drug users. Duterte is the highest-profile defendant to be tried by the ICC to date. Meanwhile, the courts of a number of countries, particularly in Europe, have invoked principles of “universal jurisdiction” to hold accountable perpetrators of grave abuses apprehended outside their own countries. Universal jurisdiction was the legal basis many years ago when Israel apprehended Adolf Eichmann and tried and executed him for his central part in carrying out the Holocaust. A more recent case involved the 1989 murder of six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper, and her daughter by the armed forces of El Salvador. Decades later a Salvadoran official implicated in the murders, Inocente Orlando Montano Morales, was discovered living in the US by the San Francisco-based Center for Justice and Accountability and extradited to Spain, where several important universal jurisdiction cases have taken place. A Spanish court convicted him and sentenced him to 133 years in prison.

Yet overall, it is impossible to say that the cause of international justice has advanced in the manner that the ICTY seemed to herald. Great crimes have been committed in recent years, or are continuing to be committed, in countries like Syria, Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Turkey, and Yemen, by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, by China against the Uyghurs, and by others elsewhere, without a meaningful prospect that the principal perpetrators will be brought to justice. With the ICC under threat from a rogue US administration, universal accountability seems still remote. In hindsight, the ICTY appears not as a forerunner to a new era but as a great exception in the history of world affairs.

entries.title: The Dartmouth Exception
entries.summary: Among its peers in the Ivy League, Dartmouth was perfectly positioned to resist Trump’s attack on higher education. It chose not to.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This essay appears, in somewhat different form, in Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, published by Penguin Press this month.

The early nineteenth century was a formative era for American higher education, a time when colleges were fragile, small-scale institutions, often caught between their colonial legacies and populist hostility to privileged elites studying the liberal arts. These tensions came to a head in the case Trustees of Dartmouth College v. Woodward, which helped to establish the independence of American higher education from governmental control. At issue was the very nature of a college. Is it a public utility, subject to the demands of the state? Or is it a self-governing institution whose autonomy deserves constitutional protection?

Dartmouth had been founded in 1769 under a royal charter from King George III, and for nearly fifty years it had operated as a private institution governed by an independent board of trustees. But in 1816 the New Hampshire legislature passed a law aimed at converting it into a state-run university. National political divisions hovered in the background. Dartmouth’s trustees were aligned with the Federalist Party. The legislature and governor were Democratic-Republicans aligned with James Monroe, who was elected president later that year; they viewed the unaccountable, elitist college with suspicion, and they planned to rewrite the charter, pack the board with political allies, and rebrand the school as “Dartmouth University.” One of the college’s own officers, William H. Woodward, defected, taking with him the financial records, the college seal, and the legal authority that went with it. The trustees sued to regain control; the case went all the way to the Supreme Court.

Their star advocate was Daniel Webster, class of 1801, a rising Federalist congressman from Massachusetts. In March 1818 he stood before the Court and argued for the college’s independence in language that was both legal and deeply personal. No transcript survives, but a witness recorded the final words of his closing statement: “It is, Sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it.” That line, now etched into the American legal imagination, reportedly brought Chief Justice John Marshall to the brink of tears. Dartmouth was not only a legal entity, it was a community, Webster argued; to tamper with it was bad law, but also a kind of betrayal.

The Dartmouth decision created a constitutional shield for all private educational institutions in the United States. In the years after the decision, colleges and universities across the country invoked the Dartmouth precedent to fend off states’ attempts to intervene in their internal affairs, from governance to curriculum to faculty appointments. The ruling helped ensure that private educational institutions would not become mere tools for the exercise of government power and that their founding documents had legal force.

The case laid the groundwork for what eventually came to be called academic freedom. Legal scholars treat Dartmouth as an early marker for institutional autonomy. The decision implied that intellectual inquiry requires distance from the state—that colleges should be places where truth is sought, not dictated. Thanks to Webster, Dartmouth’s name was immortalized not for any scientific breakthrough or curricular innovation, but for its resistance to political encroachment.

Two hundred years later, with Sian Beilock running the college, the issue of government control over academia came up once again. This time, instead of serving as a defender of American higher education as it had in the nineteenth century, Dartmouth did precisely the opposite. At a moment that demanded solidarity among threatened institutions, it eagerly bent the knee and pursued a strategy of accommodation and appeasement.

During Donald Trump’s first term, higher education emerged as a fixation for some of the president’s closest allies. Trump’s administration took aim at colleges and universities with a small tax on endowment income and gestures like the 1776 Commission, which promoted “patriotic education” as a counter to The New York Times Magazine’s 1619 Project. But these attacks were for the most part limited to blustery performances with no consistent follow-through—what the legal analyst Benjamin Wittes called “malevolence tempered by incompetence.”

Then, during Joe Biden’s presidency, protests against Israel’s war in Gaza proliferated on campuses across the country. House Republicans held high-profile hearings on antisemitism, which led to the resignations of the presidents of Harvard, Penn, and later Columbia. After the protests receded, universities felt a measure of security. This turned out to be false. On January 29, 2025, less than ten days into his second term, Trump signed an executive order called “Additional Measures to Combat Anti-Semitism.” It tasked the Departments of Education, State, Justice, and Homeland Security with making colleges and universities monitor foreign students and staff and report protesters to the government. In the words of a fact sheet accompanying Trump’s order, “To all the resident aliens who joined in the pro-jihadist protests, we put you on notice: come 2025, we will find you, and we will deport you.”

Advertisement

The administration’s new initiative quickly expanded into a sweeping federal campaign. In March the Department of Education warned schools that they must take disciplinary action against students and faculty involved in Gaza protests that it deemed antisemitic—including peaceful demonstrations critical of Israel or US foreign policy. Antisemitism was a genuine problem on many campuses, and one that many administrators were handling inadequately and inconsistently. But to the Trump administration, antisemitism was simply a cudgel to use against liberal institutions and left-wing academics. The same officials expressed no concern whatever about the rising tide of right-wing antisemitism.

Attacking universities fit neatly with Trump’s depiction of Muslim immigrants as terrorists or terrorist sympathizers. The Justice Department began investigating student organizations under material-support-for-terrorism statutes. Working in concert with the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security began revoking visas, making arrests, and attempting deportations. The campaign went far beyond trying to stamp out Gaza protests. Federal agencies demanded internal university records: admissions data disaggregated by race, sex, ethnicity, nationality, family. income, grades, and standardized test scores, as well as confidential information about faculty hiring and fundraising. Schools were ordered to shutter their diversity, equity, and inclusion offices. The most consequential change involved the enforcement of civil rights laws. Rather than initiating formal Title VI investigations—a process that would trigger administrative review—the government began treating alleged violations as grounds for immediate suspension of federal contracts and research funding. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon put it bluntly in an interview: universities could continue receiving federal funds “as long as they’re abiding by the laws and are in sync…with the administration and what the administration is trying to accomplish.” It was no longer a question of lawfulness but of political alignment.

Billions in federal research dollars were at risk. Even Harvard, the wealthiest and most powerful academic institution in the world, faced an unprecedented threat after the federal government froze more than $2.2 billion in research funding and revoked its certification to enroll international students. On April 11 Alan Garber, the university’s president, received a letter from the administration that officials subsequently claimed was an “unauthorized” draft sent in error. In exchange for allowing Harvard to keep its research funding and its foreign students, the letter demanded government supervision of its admissions policies, its faculty appointments, and even its student organizations. There were many other intolerable requirements. Harvard had to screen foreign students and reject those “hostile to… American values and institutions,” discontinue all DEI programs, and submit to a faculty plagiarism review. All of this would occur under outside supervision.

In response to the funding freeze Harvard filed suit against the government, arguing that the administration’s actions amounted to political coercion, not legitimate civil rights enforcement. Its complaint alleged that the administration’s demands were retaliatory and unconstitutional. Central to the lawsuit was a claim that the federal government was weaponizing civil rights law not to protect vulnerable groups but to control the internal operations of an independent academic institution. The suit, President and Fellows of Harvard College v. United States Department of Health and Human Services et al., marked a potential turning point in Trump’s war on higher education. Though technically about one institution, it functioned as a referendum on the future of American universities. Could they retain their autonomy under a regime determined to bring them to heel?

University presidents around the country issued statements of support for Harvard. Editorials defending the principle of academic independence appeared in major newspapers. The American Association of Colleges and Universities circulated a forceful joint letter that read:

As leaders of America’s colleges, universities, and scholarly societies, we speak with one voice against the unprecedented government overreach and political interference now endangering American higher education.

The letter’s 666 signatories included all of the other schools in the Ivy League with one notable exception: Dartmouth.

As federal immigration authorities began terminating the visas of international students across US campuses, Dartmouth set itself apart by putting its head down—and keeping it there. On April 23 Dartmouth’s president, Sian Beilock, not yet two years into the job, circulated a carefully worded internal message justifying the college’s decision to avoid taking a public stand. “As president, I have never signed open form letters because they are rarely effective tools to make change,” she wrote. “I prefer joining action-oriented coalitions, as we have done this past month as part of two successful AAU [American Association of Universities] lawsuits.”

That wasn’t true. At both Dartmouth and Barnard College, where Beilock served as president from 2017 to 2023, she had signed open letters. One denounced the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade. Another endorsed the Biden administration’s CHIPS Act and pushed for increased representation of women and people of color in engineering. The AAU lawsuits she mentioned, meanwhile, weren’t responses to the Trump administration’s attempts at political coercion. They challenged across-the-board reductions in federal reimbursement rates for research overhead—harmful to universities, yes, but universally applicable and not tied to any demands for political conformity.

The pragmatic explanation for Beilock’s restraint was that, unlike every other Ivy League school, Dartmouth had not been hit with a civil rights investigation. Nor had it suffered frozen research grants, withdrawn contracts, or visa decertifications. At least for the moment, the Trump administration was leaving Dartmouth alone. The reason, officials made clear, was the way that Beilock had handled a campus demonstration the previous spring. On May 1, 2024, students held a candlelight vigil on the Dartmouth Green to protest the war in Gaza. Large protests are rare at Dartmouth, which is more rural and has less of an activist tradition than many of its peers, and this one was tame by any standard. There were no building occupations, blocked walkways, or loudspeakers. Protesters stood in a circle, held hands, sang songs, and pitched a few tents bearing Palestinian flags and signs reading “BRAVE SPACE”—a phrase Beilock had used to describe the kind of civil dialogue she hoped to foster on divisive issues, an inversion of the “woke” demand for “safe” spaces.

Her office called the police. Within hours officers in riot gear surrounded the Green. After issuing a warning, they moved in. Eighty-nine people were arrested, including two student journalists wearing press credentials and several bystanders, one of whom suffered a broken arm. A sixty-five-year-old history professor, Annelise Orleck, who had come to observe the demonstration, was knocked to the ground and arrested—an incident caught on video. As a condition of her release, she was temporarily banned from campus. The college declined to enforce the ban but refused to drop charges against the students.

It was a grossly excessive way of dealing with a peaceful protest. The faculty voted to censure Beilock, and the student body followed suit with a no-confidence resolution. Beilock apologized, saying she hadn’t intended mass arrests or the intervention of heavily armed officers. “Part of a college president’s job is to put the safety and wellbeing of students first,” she said. “Unfortunately, my attempt to keep all of those on our campus safe made some people feel unsafe…. I am sorry for the harm this impossible decision has caused.”

But when Trump returned to power in January 2025, the overreaction Beilock regretted became an unexpected asset. It turned out that Dartmouth had an influential advocate inside the administration: Harmeet Dhillon, a Dartmouth alum now serving as assistant attorney general for civil rights. “I’m proud that Dartmouth is leading the way in dealing with antisemitism and campus unrest,” she told the alumni magazine. “I never thought I’d say those words. But I have to say, compared to the other Ivy League schools that I’m dealing with on a daily basis, Dartmouth is really one of the good guys.”

Dhillon was a classic Trump appointee: highly visible on the right, poorly suited to the position, and trailed by a disturbing past. A former Trump campaign lawyer and election denier with no prior government experience, she was also a Fox News regular—and a past editor-in-chief of The Dartmouth Review. Founded in 1980 by a group of conservative students, the Review was an early vehicle for the aggrieved style that would eventually fuel Fox and the MAGA movement. Its editors specialized in racist provocations. They mocked Black English in a 1982 column titled “Dis Sho’ Ain’t No Jive, Bro,” and in 1986 they wielded literal sledgehammers to smash anti-apartheid shanties on the Green—the Gaza tents of their day.

There was considerable irony in Dhillon serving as the face of the administration’s complaints about antisemitism. In 1988, under her editorship, the Review published a column likening Dartmouth president James O. Freedman, who was Jewish, to Adolf Hitler. The piece was so wildly offensive that it drew national coverage: it referred to Freedman as “Der Freedmann,” accused him of pursuing a “‘Final Solution’ to the Conservative Problem,” and compared his supposed right-wing victims to survivors of the Holocaust. The following issue included a cartoon of Freedman with a Hitler mustache in full Nazi regalia. Under Dhillon’s successor the paper published excerpts from Mein Kampf. Dhillon defended the column against the subsequent backlash. “This episode of public breast-beating is yet another example of the liberal hypocrisy that has been practiced and institutionalized at Dartmouth over the past generation,” she wrote. Thirty-eight years later Dhillon has yet to apologize or distance herself from an outburst of antisemitism far worse than anything that occurred at Dartmouth in the aftermath of October 7. The only change was that Jews, once her target, had become her instrument.

Dhillon’s hypocrisy put Beilock in a truly absurd position. A Jewish college president was now being hailed for standing up to antisemitism by the person responsible for the most notorious antisemitic incident in Dartmouth’s modern history. And because of her own biggest mistake on the job, which she seemed genuinely to regret, her school was enjoying an official exemption from the hell descending on its peers. Whatever her personal feelings, Beilock took the win. A few days after declining to stand with Harvard, she traveled to Washington to meet with Dhillon, after which Dhillon praised her on X: “I was so impressed to learn how Dartmouth (my alma mater) is getting it right, after all these years. Kudos to Dartmouth! I heard Jewish student applications are way up!”

Beilock worked other Washington connections as well, making at least eight trips there in 2025. To ensure that Dartmouth stayed in the Trump administration’s good graces, in March of that year she hired Matthew Raymer, an alum and the former chief counsel for the Republican National Committee, as the college’s general counsel and a member of her senior leadership team. Raymer had defended Trump’s proposal to end birthright citizenship. Now he was overseeing Dartmouth’s Office of Visa and Immigration Services. It was a strategic appointment for an institution that hoped to secure quiet exceptions to the Trump administration’s tightening anti-immigration policies.

Beilock didn’t openly take the administration’s side at any point. She subsequently signed on to an amicus brief in the Harvard suit. But that brief did not criticize the Trump administration. It made a straightforward argument that federal funding for academic research had a long history, had yielded many scientific breakthroughs, and generally benefited American society. She was, it could be argued, simply keeping her school out of trouble. As the saying goes: You don’t have to outrun the bear. You just have to outrun the other small liberal arts colleges.

Beilock is a cognitive psychologist who wrote her Ph.D. dissertation on underperformance in the face of pressure. Her argument was that performance is as much about the environment as it is about individual talent. As a junior faculty member and a vice-provost at the University of Chicago, she encouraged students to relieve stress by spending ten minutes writing about their feelings of anxiety before taking a test.

Her ideas soon found traction beyond the academy. Beilock became a sought-after speaker for businesses and sports organizations. In her first book, Choke (2010), she argued that people falter under pressure because they overmonitor routines (like making a golf putt) that should be automatic, a kind of “paralysis by analysis.” Her research made a case for DEI, examining the way that stereotyping—particularly of women and Black students—can weaken performance in math and science by diverting mental bandwidth. Her second book, How the Body Knows Its Mind (2015), extended her exploration of embodied cognition, arguing that the brain doesn’t think in isolation.

At Barnard Beilock had the chance to apply her theory that campuses are performance environments and that fostering “belonging” improves outcomes. She became fluent in the era’s social justice language. In 2020 she announced a sweeping antiracism initiative, promising

broad changes to our curriculum and academic support; new measures to recruit diverse faculty, students, and staff; re-examination of campus climate and public safety practices; and monetary and human investments.

Faculty participated in a six-week antiracism “mini-institute.” She promoted departmental antiracism statements and exempted Black, Latinx (her term), and Indigenous faculty from a hiring freeze. She created a “DEI Cabinet.” The college created a new fund for courses on race, including one Beilock championed on “chemistry and racism.”

Beilock began singing a different tune when she arrived at Dartmouth, an institution where legacy admissions outnumber African American students. Out went “underrepresented minorities,” “structural and social differences,” “antiracism,” and “privilege”; in came “civil discourse,” “institutional restraint,” and “diverse viewpoints.” When her counterparts at Harvard and Penn, Claudine Gay and Liz Magill, resigned after congressional testimony in which they sounded weak on antisemitism, Beilock took a different approach. She didn’t just change her tone. At the first sign of Gaza, she called the cops.

Her reorientation in a new political moment reflects what peers at other institutions describe as her intense ambition. It also drew on her experience at the University of Chicago, with its historic commitment to free expression and administrative neutrality. In 1967, amid the upheavals of the civil rights and Vietnam era, Chicago convened a committee chaired by the law professor Harry Kalven Jr. to articulate a position on political engagement. The Kalven Report, a two-page marvel of clarity and concision, concluded that institutional neutrality was essential to preserving free inquiry and viewpoint diversity.

After the Gaza protests and rising accusations of antisemitism on campuses nationwide, several institutions—including Princeton, Harvard, and Vanderbilt—adopted versions of the Kalven document. Daniel Diermeier, Vanderbilt’s chancellor, had appointed Beilock as Chicago’s executive vice-provost back in 2016 when he himself was provost. At Dartmouth she followed the Chicago model, pledging to refrain from official commentary on political issues. “To provide space for diverse viewpoints to be raised and fully considered, Dartmouth should exercise general restraint in issuing institutional statements,” the college’s declaration read. It was a striking evolution for a leader who, a couple of years earlier, had championed antiracism initiatives as a matter of academic responsibility.

The doctrine of institutional neutrality or “restraint” is grounded in the idea that universities best protect academic freedom by not taking sides in political debates. But in applying that doctrine at Dartmouth, Beilock appeared to miss its deeper purpose. The Kalven Report argued that neutrality exists to safeguard free inquiry, not to evade conflict. It also made clear that when a university’s central functions of teaching and research are under threat, silence is not an option. “From time to time,” the report warned,

instances will arise in which the society, or segments of it, threaten the very mission of the university and its values of free inquiry. In such a crisis, it becomes the obligation of the university as an institution to oppose such measures and actively to defend its interests and its values.

That line was written with the memory of McCarthyism still fresh. Kalven’s goal was for the university to protect free speech, not to provide an excuse to keep silent about the freedom of its faculty and students. Dartmouth’s statement on institutional restraint does contain a version of the Kalven exception but renders it in lifeless legalese: “When confronted with issues directly relating to Dartmouth’s mission, senior leaders will reaffirm Dartmouth’s core values and commit to taking actions in support thereof.”

The challenge for Dartmouth was that its values were under threat, but indirectly. The Trump administration’s 2025 actions struck at the foundations of higher education as a whole: who gets admitted, what gets taught, which ideas can be researched, who can speak. It was a campaign of coercion far more menacing than what happened during the McCarthy era because of the way the expansion of federal funding had increased the government’s leverage in the intervening seventy-five years. But the government wasn’t threatening to put Dartmouth itself out of business. Because of a confluence of circumstances—Beilock’s misjudged crackdown and Harmeet Dhillon’s favoritism—Dartmouth got a hall pass and was taking full advantage of it. By staying quiet, Dartmouth sent a powerful signal throughout a wider academic community that was struggling to form a unified front. The message was that individual self-preservation mattered more than solidarity or fundamental beliefs.

In September 2025 US District Court Judge Allison D. Burroughs handed a victory to Harvard, ruling that the Trump administration’s actions amounted to “retaliation, unconstitutional conditions, and unconstitutional coercion.” But the victory did little to solve Harvard’s problems. Instead it underscored just how much power a hostile federal government could wield to punish disobedience. The administration said it would appeal, and there was no assurance that a sympathetic Supreme Court wouldn’t ultimately endorse the government’s view that it could simply declare Harvard noncompliant and cut off all its funding. Meanwhile Trump’s team held plenty of other cards. It could delay or deny grants, or initiate audits and investigations. In the middle of the lawsuit Kristi Noem, then secretary of homeland security, revoked Harvard’s authorization to enroll international students, a devastating blow for a research university.

Harvard managed to secure a temporary restraining order but still faced a protracted court battle, as well as the very real possibility that DHS would simply sidestep the ruling by delaying visa approvals. If Harvard kept fighting, it risked legal costs in the hundreds of millions, endless compliance demands from federal agencies, reputational damage, and significant disruption to international recruitment. It was a bleak prospect. In February 2026, after The New York Times reported that Trump was offering to drop his demand that Harvard pay a $200 million fine, he became enraged and raised his settlement price to $1 billion.

As the most prominent institution in American higher education, Harvard’s response would set the pattern for all the other holdouts. When Harvard had a good day in court, other universities were emboldened to hold the line. But when word spread that it was close to striking a deal, the mood shifted. If Harvard, backed by a $57 billion endowment, couldn’t resist the administration, how could anyone else? Trump understood this. He wanted a settlement that would send a clear message to the rest of the academy: Harvard had to give in, so you do too.

No college can withstand a systemic political assault alone, especially one backed by control over funding, visas, and regulatory oversight. The strength of academic freedom has always depended on unity and collective resolve. Every separate peace with Trump weakened the positions of those standing firm. Each capitulation—first Columbia, then Brown, then several others including Penn, Cornell, and Northwestern—allowed the administration to portray the remaining opposition as marginal and weak rather than united by principle.

Dartmouth’s Dhillon exemption put it in the strongest position to stand up for its peer institutions. Dartmouth has around seven thousand students, two thirds of them undergraduates, and no sprawling assortment of graduate schools. Instead it has three second-tier professional schools: engineering, medicine, and business. As a result, it doesn’t receive much federal research funding, and its finances are otherwise impregnable. Its $9 billion endowment works out to about $1.3 million per student. In practice, endowment funds are largely restricted and don’t support general operations or academic freedom emergencies. But differences in institutional structure and wealth still matter. Research-focused institutions like Harvard (with around 17,000 graduate students out of 24,000 in total) depend much more heavily on federal dollars. In 2024 Dartmouth took in $160 million in government contracts and research funding, which was less than 10 percent of its operating budget. Financial dependence gives Washington enormous leverage over large research universities—and far less over undergraduate-centered colleges like Dartmouth.

The same holds for visas. Twenty-one percent of Dartmouth’s student body is international, compared with 28 percent at Harvard. Because international students typically pay full tuition, having fewer of them means less financial risk from government meddling with visas. So while Dartmouth lacks Harvard’s size or global stature, it was in a much better position to resist government pressure. That made its silence all the more disappointing. Dartmouth had the leeway to be brave, yet it chose not to be.

Rejecting Trump’s malicious intervention doesn’t mean pretending that American higher education is perfect. The administration’s attacks contained many valid points of criticism—about Gaza protests that crossed the line into antisemitic harassment, the inconsistent application of free speech principles, excesses of identity politics, and ballooning student debt. But the answer to higher education’s shortcomings isn’t authoritarian coercion.

In October 2025, as legal and political pressure escalated, the Department of Education unveiled what came to be known as the Offer. Trump’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education” presented itself as a sweeping blueprint for restoring meritocratic and apolitical values to American universities. In return for privileged access to federal funding, universities would be required to adopt a set of policies aligned with the administration’s agenda. Among other requirements, the compact demanded that universities cap international undergraduate enrollment at 15 percent; eliminate race and gender identity as factors in admissions, financial aid, and hiring; and submit to ideological audits, donor disclosure, and requirements to report protesters to the government.

Another clause required that signatories remake or abolish “institutional units that purposefully punish, belittle, and even spark violence against conservative ideas,” which sounded like it could turn mockery of Republicans into a punishable offense. Violations could trigger retroactive clawbacks, including the loss of all federal funds received during the year of the breach, plus private gifts secured in the same period. The carrot for agreeing to all of that was priority approval for research funding and continued authorization to enroll international students.

By then the familiar Trump-supporting billionaires were all popping out of the woodwork. Stephen Schwarzman was serving as a back-channel negotiator between Trump and Harvard. Marc Rowan, the private equity billionaire who had pressured Penn’s board to fire Liz Magill, had worked with the White House Domestic Policy Council to draft the compact. What the nine schools that received the Offer had in common was that the Trump administration thought they were pliable. Brown, Penn, and the University of Virginia had already cut deals with the government; Dartmouth and Vanderbilt had declared policies of institutional neutrality (or “restraint,” in Dartmouth’s case) and were seen as Trump-friendly; the University of Arizona and the University of Texas at Austin faced pressure from Republican state legislatures; and MIT and USC were both deeply dependent on federal contracts and research funding.

Most of the responses were immediate and unequivocal. MIT president Sally Kornbluth—the only survivor of Elise Stefanik’s 2023 congressional inquisition—was the first to say no. Her letter to Linda McMahon rejected the offer as incompatible with academic freedom and scientific integrity. She said that MIT didn’t want preferential treatment. “Scientific funding,” she wrote, “should be based on scientific merit alone.” Brown, Penn, USC, and UVA quickly followed with similar rejections.

Dartmouth moved more slowly. According to someone familiar with the internal deliberations, Beilock and the Dartmouth board found some of the content of the compact unacceptable. But her rejection of it, which finally came on October 18, 2025, wasn’t resounding, it was a simpering word salad:

I welcome further engagement around how we can (a) enhance the long-standing partnership between the federal government and this country’s leading research universities and (b) ensure that higher education stays focused on academic excellence….

We remain open to other ways to work with the federal government to enhance higher education.

Welcoming further engagement and finding other ways to work with the Trump administration? For an academic institution, it was like welcoming the ten plagues and asking for a few more. In the face of authoritarian bullying, fawning doesn’t protect you. It simply invites more coercion.

entries.title: An Ecosystem of Her Own
entries.summary: Maren Hassinger’s alchemical touch transforms the most resistant materials into evocations of the endlessly changing natural world.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In Maren Hassinger’s hands, bits of frayed industrial wire pinned to a wall come to resemble dandelion bristles carried away by the breeze. Wire cables, arranged in clusters across a gallery floor, conjure tufts of grass. And weighty ropes—the sort that might be used to moor a boat—are braided with chains and arranged on the ground in the form of a curving river.

The products of Hassinger’s alchemical touch are on view in a resplendent exhibition at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA), her most comprehensive retrospective to date. The show is roughly chronological, charting her career from her native Los Angeles to New York, where she continues to make work at the age of seventy-nine. At the University of California Botanical Garden, two miles away from the museum, stands a recent sculpture called Monument (Pyramid) (2022/2026), a ten-foot-tall pyramid made of woven redwood branches. Its woodsy setting is fitting for an artist who has, over the course of her career, regularly turned to nature for both materials and ideas. Even her works made with processed matter can call to mind phenomena like the current of a stream or a gust of wind. In Beach (1980), which consumes several dozen square feet at BAMPFA, slender, hip-height wooden rods fixed in plaster bases tilt like tall grasses rustled by a breeze.

It was by stumbling into dead ends that Hassinger found her métier as a sculptor. In 1965 she left Los Angeles for Bennington College in Vermont, intending to study dance, one of the institution’s more renowned programs. Told by her professors that she lacked technical proficiency, she was steered toward sculpture instead, and she learned to make abstract geometric works inspired by Anthony Caro and David Smith, both of whom had taught at Bennington. She was then rejected by the graduate program in sculpture at UCLA, but her work caught the eye of the ceramicist and textile designer Bernard Kester, who became known for curating the influential 1971 exhibition “Deliberate Entanglements,” which highlighted the sculptural potential of weaving. He had established the school’s fiber arts program, where Hassinger ultimately enrolled and began to incorporate elements of textile production, such as knotting, into her work.

The curators of “Living Moving Growing” have done an admirable job of pulling together a body of work that defies easy categorization. Hassinger came of artistic age during the height of the Black Arts Movement. She was part of a loose community of Black artists in Los Angeles in the 1970s that included David Hammons, Houston Conwill, and Senga Nengudi, who were, in varying ways, merging sculpture, abstraction, video, and performance. But Hassinger’s early work didn’t directly make use of the typical signifiers of the African American experience, and even in those early years she stood apart for her interest in permanence and scale.

Her sculptures can form their own discrete mini-ecosystems—Untitled (1972), for example, features a dozen industrial ropes dangling in a small gallery like elegant microbial forms—but she has also used her pieces as settings for performances. Included in the show are striking pictures taken in the 1970s by the Los Angeles photographer Adam Avila that show Hassinger and others dancing among her installations of tree branches and undulating strands of cable.

Her interest in experimentation has not dulled over time. One gallery wall is covered in inflated pink plastic bags, an installation titled Love (2008), offering a startling burst of color that nods at environmental degradation. Also on view are a number of videos, including Wind (2013), created in collaboration with her daughter, Ava Hassinger. The pair, dressed in loose white clothing evocative of Afro-Caribbean spiritual traditions, advance along a wild shore, the wind whipping up their ensembles. There is billowing movement even when they stand still.

No single category can contain Hassinger, and neither can any one museum. Some of her most significant sculptures are too large to be displayed simultaneously at BAMPFA. Missing, for example, is the installation Walking (1978), composed of dozens of clusters of cables bundled together to resemble a forest of roots. But this is a quibble, and the curators are right to let many of her other works breathe. With their inventive and graceful incorporation of natural materials and forms, they are quietly seductive, and they function as a warning: touch grass before it’s buried in steel and concrete.

entries.title: The Village Photographer
entries.summary: Madeleine de Sinéty sloughed off her aristocratic upbringing and spent her life capturing small-town life in Brittany and Maine.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
One July day in 1972, a French photographer named Madeleine de Sinéty got stuck in traffic on her way back to Paris from the countryside. “I left the jammed highway for a small country road,” she later remembered, “and decided to stop for the night in the most out-of-the way village I could find.” The tiny farming settlement of Poilley, in Brittany, would become her home for the next eight years, and the subject of more than 50,000 intimate, often unsettling photographs. Sinéty developed a knack for finding within quotidian domestic and village scenes—a woman brushing her hair, a picnic in the sun—a dreamlike sense of mystery.

Sinéty’s first retrospective, on view now at the Jeu de Paume, marks a growing interest in an artist whose work was barely published, and only twice exhibited, in her lifetime. (She died in 2011.) Like her American contemporaries Saul Leiter and Joel Meyerowitz, Sinéty shot color photographs in a soft yet vivid palette. In Poilley she was especially drawn to the chaotic and the surreal: pigs butchered on kitchen tables next to bored kids; toddlers hacking away at apple trees with long wooden poles; a lordly gray-haired woman in a floral dress and sunglasses presiding over the harvest, issuing orders from the top of a haystack.

Sinéty had taken up photography just a few years before she stumbled into her new life in the village. Born into an aristocratic family in the Loire Valley in 1934, she married her first husband in 1960, separated from him in 1968, and met her second, the American journalist Daniel Behrman, in Paris a year later. The pair shared a love of train travel, and together they set out to document the last steam train lines in France. Behrman wrote a series of articles for the magazine Réalités, and Sinéty, with her first camera, took the pictures. They befriended drivers and mechanics at the Gare Montparnasse and hitched rides out into the countryside. Sinéty photographed not only the spectacular trains, with their glowing coal furnaces wreathed in smoke, but also charismatic, grease-stained operators; drivers juggling childcare and paperwork; and families of railway employees living in the shadows of the train lines. In one photograph, a typical kitchen scene—with a broom, a jug, a dog, a woman reading the paper, and a small girl regarding the camera—is cut through by an approaching steam train framed by the open back door, seemingly on a collision course with the house’s unwitting occupants.

Sinéty then moved to Poilley. (Behrman commuted from Paris every weekend bearing fresh packets of slide film.) When she first arrived, she wrote, a resident named Maria Touchard “watched me suspiciously as I hesitantly walked down the dirt path that led to the farm.” Touchard had reason to be suspicious: Sinéty came from a world of châteaux and Swiss nannies, and she might have treated the villagers like specimens of sociological or anthropological observation. Gradually, however, her project became theirs too. Her photographs were viewed regularly during raucous late-night slideshows in the village hall. “It was a joyful and noisy gathering,” Sinéty wrote in her journal after one such evening. “Everyone had red faces and shining eyes, and they shouted and cheered as each photo appeared.” When Sinéty’s first son was born in Poilley in 1976, she asked Touchard—now a close friend—to be his godmother.

In 1980, with Behrman growing older, the family moved to California and then to the small town of Rangeley, Maine, not far from the Canadian border. Sinéty contributed to the local newspaper, The Rangeley Highlander, while taking black-and-white photographs of life in the town, just as she had done in Poilley. All her obsessions remained alive and well, from the disquieting mixture of brutality and tenderness with which humans treat animals to the dreamworlds inhabited by children and the transfixing peculiarity of adult social rituals, such as a grim-faced Nativity procession down a snowy road at night.

Sinéty was diagnosed with breast cancer in 1986, and Behrman with lung cancer soon after. She survived for another twenty-five years, but Behrman died swiftly. In 1990, widowed and working as a photojournalist and wedding photographer in Maine, Sinéty received a letter from the mayor of Poilley. The villagers, he informed her, had pooled enough money to fly her back. Things were changing there, and they needed her to photograph them one last time, “before it’s too late.” Back to Poilley she went.
