entries.title: Unraveling Medical Mysteries
entries.summary: Patients with undiagnosed conditions suffer not only from their symptoms but also from the uncertainly of not knowing what afflicts them.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Patients without a diagnosis live in a medical purgatory. Their failure to receive one may be attributed to their having vague symptoms, such as a general feeling of malaise, weakness, or fluctuating muscle pain. They usually consult their primary care doctor, who, unable to provide a diagnosis, refers them to specialists: neurologists, gastroenterologists, rheumatologists, hematologists, cardiologists. Desperation fills their lives, amplified by physicians who dismiss their complaints as psychosomatic—in their heads—and then prescribe medications for mental health conditions, such as Prozac or Valium. Not infrequently, when a person’s symptoms are seen as manifestations of stress and anxiety, Alexandra Sifferlin writes in her engaging and illuminating The Elusive Body, it makes “getting a diagnosis deeply complicated and rife with uncertainty.” Doctors often retreat from continuing to care for such patients, frustrated that despite a physical exam and blood tests and scans they are unable to offer an answer. And without one, treatment becomes guesswork, ineffective at best, harmful at worst. Patients without a diagnosis typically feel they have exhausted every resource and don’t know where to turn.

The centerpiece of The Elusive Body is the Undiagnosed Disease Program (UDP) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). It serves, Sifferlin writes, as “a clinic of last resort,” bringing together a team of physicians and researchers who try to unravel a patient’s mysterious condition by applying advanced technologies, particularly genetic analysis. They don’t always succeed in providing an answer, but when they do, even in the absence of an effective therapy, there is meaningful relief for patients who learn it’s not all in their heads.

The plight of Louise Proctor, a woman with an undiagnosed malady, spans many pages in the book and poignantly illustrates the physical and psychological vicissitudes of life in medical purgatory. Her odyssey began in 1980, when she was twenty-five and working full-time in a family services office in rural Kentucky. Her job, entering data into spreadsheets from food stamp and welfare applications, was mostly sedentary. One lunch break she found that she could hardly climb a familiar hill. The pain began in her toes and moved up her legs: “When she bent down to massage the muscle in her left calf, she nearly cried out in agony. Her leg felt as hard as a rock.”

In the ensuing years, such episodes occurred frequently. Her legs felt as though they were “turning to stone,” and as her condition worsened, her strength waned. Louise consulted numerous physicians. She was told that her leg pain was caused by insufficient exercise, possibly by arthritis, or even by secondhand smoke. But despite her exercising more, eating well, and taking prescribed medications for arthritis, her symptoms did not abate. Outwardly nothing seemed wrong with her legs. Repeatedly told that she just needed to walk more, she felt that her condition was being attributed to her sloth. “I knew something was wrong,” she told Sifferlin in a later interview. “I wasn’t imagining it.” For three decades, as her legs repeatedly froze, Louise did not receive a diagnosis. “The mystery deepened when her four siblings also began experiencing similar symptoms,” Sifferlin writes.

Louise’s life became even more fraught when her baby daughter, Suzanne, didn’t gain weight. Initially, as in Louise’s case, there was no diagnosis, but then the two of them went to a medical center in Lexington, Kentucky, and Suzanne was told she had cystic fibrosis. This is a genetic disorder that affects the transport of ions such as chloride in vital tissues, including the lungs, pancreas, and intestines. Mucus builds up, impairing breathing and damaging organs.

“These two Proctor women exemplify just how powerful a diagnosis can be,” Sifferlin writes.

Suzanne’s awful symptoms and poor prognosis were at least explained. With that certainty, she and her mother could see what lay ahead, and that clarity gave Suzanne a kind of peace. It also focused her doctors’ efforts: Having a diagnosis meant Suzanne’s medical team knew what they were dealing with, and what treatments they could try. Louise, meanwhile, was languishing without one.

Suzanne died at the age of fifteen. After her death, Louise decided “to confront the mystery of her own body once more.” She eventually saw Dr. Karen Saylor, a family physician, who listened attentively as she described how she could not do daily chores such as laundry, walk up a driveway, or keep up with her family on a visit to a zoo. Dr. Saylor sent Louise to the hospital for imaging. It had been many years since she had stood frozen in pain on that familiar hill, and this was the first time a doctor had ordered imaging (which shows how glibly her complaints had been dismissed). The result of the ultrasound “was shocking: Louise’s arteries all around her knee were lined with hardened calcium.” She thought to herself, “I’ve been trying to tell everyone something was wrong, and no one would listen.”

Advertisement

A doctor’s ego may be an obstacle to admitting being stumped in making a diagnosis. Dr. Saylor, on the other hand, was willing to acknowledge that she was clueless after the ultrasound and sought help to find answers. She found that there was a team of physicians and researchers “who focused on the most complex medical cases that baffle physicians across the United States”—the UDP—and she sent Louise’s and her sister’s medical histories, the ultrasound and X-rays, and other records to the NIH.

The UDP had been open for only a year when Dr. Saylor reached out to its director, Dr. William Gahl, a pediatrician and geneticist who focused on rare diseases and had been the clinical director of the National Human Genome Research Institute of the NIH. “People with rare diseases feel the limits of the diagnostic process most acutely,” Sifferlin notes. Because these patients have diseases that are less familiar to health care professionals, they often end up languishing for long periods without a diagnosis or are misdiagnosed and receive incorrect treatments. The UDP was founded not only to provide answers to patients who had sought diagnoses for years; it also reflected the NIH’s primary research mission by discovering new diseases, launching clinical trials, and connecting patients with others who share a rare disorder. (The UDP was ultimately expanded to the Undiagnosed Diseases Network—UDN—to include academic centers beyond the NIH, particularly those with expertise in genetics, such as Harvard and Baylor.)

The UDP was the first resource of its kind in the United States. It was launched in May 2008 and in the first two weeks more than two hundred prospective patients called; it since has received thousands of applications. How to triage these applications was a challenge. Dr. Gahl said that his team was looking for clues from the patients’ stories, physical examinations, and laboratory tests, in search of “a new, unique, or remarkable physical finding or constellation of such findings.” A medical board of NIH experts reviewed the cases and then invited selected patients for a weeklong visit, during which they would undergo testing and be seen by a team of specialists in different disciplines. To be admitted to the program, the applicant “didn’t just have to be sick and not know why,” Sifferlin writes. “Their illness had to be unique enough to go undiagnosed, while also potentially bearing on a more widespread health problem.”

Louise Proctor’s case was new to Dr. Gahl and his colleagues. They had never seen X-rays and ultrasound images that showed deposits of calcium as extensive as those in her and her siblings’ limbs. Blood was reaching Louise’s legs only through collateral vessels that had developed to bypass the blockages and were too limited to allow blood to flow normally, thus causing severe pain and limited mobility.

The fact that Louise’s four siblings were experiencing similar symptoms, Sifferlin writes, “suggested a possible genetic link.” The UDP’s geneticists were uniquely suited to explore their mysterious malady. In May 2009 the entire Proctor family gathered at the headquarters of the UDP in Bethesda, Maryland. “By this point,” Sifferlin notes, “all five siblings struggled to walk more than one to six blocks without pain.” They underwent an extensive evaluation, including X-rays, PET scans, CT scans, ultrasounds, and, most critically, genetic analysis. The sequencing of the human genome had been completed by 2003, and in 2009, as Dr. Gahl was reviewing the Proctors’ application, there was a push to sequence the DNA of more people to better understand genetic variation and illness. The Proctors were accepted into the UDP.

“A healthy person’s blood vessels should look like a garden hose,” Sifferlin writes. “But the blood vessels of Louise and her siblings were shockingly obstructed by calcium.” As it happened, a vascular specialist at the NIH had a postdoctoral fellow, Dr. Cynthia St. Hilaire, working in his laboratory. After seeing Louise’s CT scan, “she felt a twinge of recognition.” Dr. St. Hilaire had done her Ph.D. work on a protein called the adenosine receptor. One of its functions is to control the constriction and relaxation of blood vessels. Her studies included genetically engineered mice that allowed the researchers to see the function of the protein by deleting the gene. The mice without the adenosine receptor had characteristics that resembled what Dr. St. Hilaire saw in the Proctor siblings’ legs. “It seemed far too serendipitous that her incredibly narrow area of Ph.D. research would apply to her first case acting as a consultant for the UDP,” Sifferlin writes. The members of the Proctor family each underwent a skin biopsy that extracted from their arms a small piece of tissue about the size of a pencil eraser for further laboratory study.

Advertisement

Both Proctor parents were healthy. Each presumably had one copy of the mutated gene and one copy of the intact gene, which indicated that the trait was recessive. But “each of their children may have inherited two copies of the mutated gene, one from each parent, which resulted in their symptoms.” The UDP team learned that the parents were third cousins, increasing the likelihood that they shared a recessive mutated gene.

The team initially identified ninety-two genes that they suspected could contain the sought-after mutation. Dr. St. Hilaire examined the list and saw a gene for CD73. “She was shocked because CD73 is the main enzyme that produces adenosine, the molecule that binds and activates the receptor she had studied during her Ph.D. program.” When the researchers analyzed the proteins from the skin cells, they found that the Proctor siblings had no CD73. “Holy shit, holy shit, holy shit,” Dr. St. Hilaire whispered to herself. “There’s no CD73 there.” It turned out that a gene responsible for producing CD73 was mutated. The team could now definitively say that the lack of CD73 was the cause of calcium deposits in the Proctor siblings’ arteries. “This was the answer. It was a truly novel disease discovery,” Sifferlin writes.

The UDP identified nine people who had the mutation and similar symptoms: the five Proctor siblings, three sisters in Italy, and one person in San Francisco. The researchers named the condition arterial calcification due to deficiency of CD73 (ACDC). The findings were published in The New England Journal of Medicine in February 2011.

For the Proctor siblings the findings afforded an understanding of what was afflicting their bodies. “It was all a bit mind-blowing,” said Louise’s sister Elizabeth. “It’s nice to know why I am having this pain, and that it’s not because I am out of shape. I am not crazy and there is a medical reason for this.” After decades of appointments and being dismissed, this was a true diagnosis. Although there is not yet a specific therapy for ACDC, simply knowing what is wrong moves a patient out of purgatory as scientists work on finding an effective treatment.

A few years later Dr. St. Hilaire published a study showing that the kind of calcification experienced by the Proctor siblings is a more serious form of the calcification experienced by millions of people with more common peripheral vascular disease. ACDC involves calcification of blood vessels and although rare is relevant to patients with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and hypertension who also suffer disabling vascular impairment. An estimated eight million people forty and older in the United States have a related condition. “That’s one thing people don’t fully appreciate,” said Dr. St. Hilaire. While the Proctor calcification is rare and aggressive, Sifferlin writes, “the underlying mechanisms are shared among people with less severe but still debilitating artery disease—they also have low CD73.” Dr. St. Hilaire’s laboratory is hoping to use the knowledge gained from the UDP discovery to treat other vascular diseases.

Patients who are incorrectly diagnosed occupy a parallel purgatory to those without a diagnosis, because they also lack an accurate picture of their disorder. Their symptoms, like those of patients without a diagnosis, persist as doctors prescribe ineffective or harmful therapies. Between 10 and 15 percent of all patients are estimated to be misdiagnosed or suffer a serious delay in diagnosis. Some of these data come from studies that found that the true cause of the disorder was revealed only by an autopsy.

Sifferlin touches on the cognitive pitfalls that can result in misdiagnosis. The work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in identifying and characterizing heuristics and biases, which often occur under conditions of uncertainty and time pressure—both prevalent in medicine—can explain much of flawed clinical reasoning. Dr. Pat Croskerry, an emergency room physician in Nova Scotia who has a Ph.D. in psychology in addition to his medical degree, developed a catalog of biases in medicine. For example, doctors may seize on the first symptom offered by the patient or the first abnormal laboratory finding—so-called anchoring—and then follow a path of thinking that ignores other salient information. Anchoring fixes the physician’s mind on a single diagnosis that all too often is wrong. Another common bias is known as availability. Here the physician’s thinking is guided by what is most available in their mind, often a dramatic case or a recent series of similar patients, as in the midst of a flu epidemic. In such cases the physician ignores the alternative diagnoses that should be considered.

A third kind of misguided thinking is attribution bias: the tendency to blame people rather than circumstances when things go wrong, for example by invoking negative stereotypes. A disheveled man, unshaven, with an enlarged liver, may be designated a drunk with alcoholic cirrhosis, although in fact he has an inherited liver disorder and does not drink to excess.

While working on my book How Doctors Think (2007), I had the opportunity to interview scores of patients and physicians in an effort to illustrate each of these cognitive biases with real-world cases. I recount in my writing several of my own misdiagnoses when I fell into cognitive traps. As a resident in training, I saw an elderly woman with diabetes who complained of abdominal pain. I anchored on gastroparesis, a slowly emptying, bloated stomach, which is a common diagnosis in diabetics. I missed the serious underlying cause of her pain: an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Fortunately she survived my mistake.

Sifferlin briefly mentions how to protect against some cognitive biases. She raises the question inherent in metacognition—thinking about your thinking—that clinicians should pose to themselves: What else could it be? But it’s important to ask whether there are any data from the patient’s history, physical exam, laboratory testing, X-rays, and scans that do not fit into the working diagnosis. Moreover, it is also important to question Occam’s razor, taught in medical training, which posits that there should be a single unifying hypothesis that accounts for a constellation of findings. Human biology does not conform to such a paradigm of logic, since often there is more than one cause for diverse symptoms. This protects against doctors stopping their thinking when they find the first diagnosis; if they are too satisfied in their search, they miss a second possible diagnosis or even a third.

After Donald Trump took office for the second time in January 2025, he and the Department of Government Efficiency, initially headed by Elon Musk, began cutting federal funding for scientific and medical research, including for the NIH. There was concern that the UDN could be closed down, Sifferlin writes:

The saving grace has been the patients. They’ve formed advocacy groups and worked hard to keep the program running, including calling on members of Congress. The goodwill the US government earns from taking medical mysteries seriously is hard to overstate. UDN has successfully diagnosed hundreds of Americans, and it builds trust in a health system that badly needs it.

While the program is focused on rare and undiagnosed diseases,

it has become a model for how to approach difficult diagnoses broadly. It emphasizes teamwork, deep dives into each person’s medical history, and long appointments that combine cutting-edge science with the trust-building elements of good bedside care.

There is a certain irony here, since the UDN draws on the most advanced medical technologies—detailed genetic analysis, sophisticated scans, comprehensive blood tests. But as Louise Proctor’s case showed, unraveling a medical mystery begins in the old-fashioned way—by taking the patient seriously.

entries.title: Cherchez les Femmes
entries.summary: A new initiative at the Prado calls visitors’ attention to the many works in the collection acquired by royal women.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In 2022 Madrid’s Museo Nacional del Prado introduced a new initiative to guide visitors through its vast galleries: “The Female Perspective” (El Prado en femenino), which highlights all the ways in which women have shaped its holdings as collectors and sponsors of art (promotoras artísticas). Curiously, in English we call these promotoras “patronesses” of the arts rather than “matrons,” as if such activities were a fatherly action more naturally suited to men. The Prado’s collection, however, tells quite another story. A short film narrated by Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the University of Murcia and the director of “The Female Perspective,” shows what the museum’s galleries would look like if the works acquired by women were removed: a series of yawning gaps and blank walls (albeit walls recently painted in the strong, striking colors that the Prado’s director, Miguel Falomir Faus, has introduced to complement both the artworks and the lofty spaces). Tellingly, the camera moves to the clack of high heels to show that the film “sees” its subject explicitly through women’s eyes.

Through a series of find-it-yourself maps, “The Female Perspective” has connected promotoras artísticas from the fifteenth through the eighteenth centuries with the works they bought, inherited, or commissioned—a hunt for treasure that leads visitors to well-known masterpieces but also to gems long buried by lack of attention rather than layers of dirt. These itineraries, clever and unfailingly rewarding, have made the initiative a great success. As a more permanent legacy, the museum has produced companion volumes for each of the three itineraries introduced in 2022, 2024, and 2026. They contain miniature versions of the maps as well as brief accounts of the patronesses and the objects they added to the collection.

The earliest promotoras were all royal; the Museo Nacional del Prado was founded in 1819 as the Royal Museum (shortly thereafter renamed the National Museum of Paintings and Sculptures) to share the Spanish crown’s vast artistic holdings with the public. The women featured in “The Female Perspective,” many of them eventually rulers in their own right, made their way successfully through a system of government that drove other women of their rank to madness, misery, and isolation; they displayed an astonishing ability to adapt to new environments, new languages, and treacherous courts. Their first duty as royal wives—often married in their teens—may have been to bear the next generation of European rulers, but in theory they were also expected to govern their realms in their husbands’ absences. Much to the surprise of the male ministers who surrounded them, the women featured in this series also governed in fact.

The Female Perspective: Women Art Patrons of the Museo del Prado (1451–1633) begins, like the Kingdom of Spain, with Isabella I of Castile, who united two Iberian kingdoms and created the modern Spanish state when at the age of eighteen she married the fifteen-year-old Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469. The last surviving heirs of their respective branches of the Trastámara dynasty, they were also cousins, and hence they required a papal dispensation to marry; when Pope Paul II refused to oblige, a suitable document was simply forged in his name. Isabella continued to rule Castile in her own right, while Ferdinand retained his hold on Aragon; together they were known as Their Most Catholic Majesties. (The two realms were not officially conjoined until the eighteenth century.) To secure their claims to their respective thrones, the couple moved constantly from city to city without ever establishing a single capital.

Castile was the wealthier state, and Isabella in many ways was the dominant partner in the marriage. A portrait from 1490 by an anonymous Flemish painter conveys her majesty—that is, her authority—as regal reserve. Isabella’s wealth and rank show forth in her damask gown and an elaborate pendant, a gift from her father and hence a tangible token of her right as a woman to claim the throne, but other details—the garment’s modest cut, the simple hairstyle, the unobtrusive prayer book she has closed over one finger to mark her place—suggest that she carries out her responsibilities with piety and practicality. She averts her dark-ringed eyes from the viewer, but they are not downcast; Isabella is a queen, after all, subordinate to no one but the God who anointed her.

Isabella’s artistic tastes ran to Flemish masters such as her anonymous portraitist and the equally anonymous, moderately talented painter of The Virgin of the Catholic Monarchs (1491–1493), which shows the royal couple and their two eldest children, Juan and Isabella, kneeling before an enthroned Virgin and Child. Four members of the Dominican Order flank the royal family: Saint Dominic, the theologian Thomas Aquinas, the thirteenth-century Italian inquisitor known as Peter Martyr (Pietro da Verona), identified by his wounded scalp and the sword plunged into his chest, and, behind Ferdinand, the notorious Tomás de Torquemada, the first Grand Inquisitor of the Spanish Inquisition, an institution established by Their Most Catholic Majesties in 1480 to ensure that converts from Judaism and Islam in formerly multicultural Spain did not fall back into their old faiths. Under their rule, with the devout Isabella as the driving force, Spanish society took an increasingly intolerant turn: in 1492 Ferdinand conquered Granada, the peninsula’s last Islamic city-state, Isabella sent Columbus across the ocean in search of wealth and new converts, and Their Most Catholic Majesties expelled the Jews from Spain.

Advertisement

In part because of the confused struggle to establish the successor to Ferdinand and Isabella, the monarchy’s first large-scale collector, male or female, was the remarkable Mary of Hungary, one of six children born in Flanders to Their Most Catholic Majesties’ daughter Juana and her husband, the dashing Habsburg heir Philip, Duke of Burgundy, known as Philip the Fair. Their marriage in 1496 added the Low Countries to the Spanish dominions and the distinctive Habsburg physiognomy to the Trastámara gene pool. Mary, the couple’s fifth child and third daughter, barely saw either of her parents. Philip died in 1506, a year after her birth, and Juana was declared mad and permanently confined in 1509 when Mary was four. Together with three of her five siblings, she grew up with their aunt, the Archduchess Margaret of Austria, Philip’s twice-widowed sister, who served the Holy Roman Empire as regent of the Netherlands from 1507 to 1530.

One of the most respected rulers of early modern Europe and a woman of famously independent spirit, Margaret was also a conscientious guardian of her titled brood, ensuring each child an excellent education (which included the handling of weaponry, economics, and military strategy for the girls as well as the boys) and an advantageous marriage. Mary, destined since birth for Louis II Jagiellon of Hungary as a way of reinforcing the long-standing Habsburg connection to Eastern Europe, was married by proxy in 1515 at the age of ten, but only went to live with her husband in 1521 and was officially crowned queen of Bohemia in 1522. The pair fell deeply in love, but in 1526 Louis died in battle against the Ottoman troops of Suleiman the Magnificent. Devastated, Mary tried to persuade her brother Ferdinand I to take charge of Hungary, but instead, as the newly crowned king of Bohemia (succeeding the slain Louis), he appointed her regent of her adopted country. She was twenty-one. She ruled Hungary until 1531, when her eldest brother, Charles, long since anointed as Holy Roman Emperor (as Charles V) and king of Spain (as Charles I), summoned her to replace their beloved aunt Margaret as governor of the Netherlands.

Mary governed the Low Countries for twenty-four years with a cool head and careful attention to finance, all the while amassing her impressive collection of art. Notably she commissioned works by Italian as well as Flemish masters and thereby exerted a defining influence on subsequent royal taste. In 1555, when Charles resigned his imperial title and withdrew to the Spanish monastery of Yuste, Mary, now fifty, asked to be relieved of her position as well. She retired with some trepidation to Spain to be near her sister Leonor (who had retired to Castile after the death of her second husband, François I of France) and took up residence in the castle of Cigales near Valladolid, staying well clear of her nephew Philip II, the new king of Spain. When Mary died in 1558, her collection passed to the crown. She and Philip may have disagreed on religion (Mary had been in contact with Martin Luther) and politics, but they shared a passion for Titian and the old masters of the German and Netherlandish tradition.

A pair of sixteenth-century marble busts of the two retired widows are displayed in the Prado’s Room 56. Leonor’s bust has been attributed to the Flemish sculptor and architect Jacques Dubroeucq, who designed Mary’s palace in the Belgian city of Binche as a rival to the French royal residence of Fontainebleau (it was vindictively demolished in 1554 by the French king Henri II) and taught the Flemish sculptor Jean de Boulogne, who found fame in Florence as Giambologna. Mary’s bust is ascribed to the Italian sculptor Leone Leoni and his son Pompeo. Both women are dressed in widow’s weeds, with an unflattering white cloth pulled down over their heads, but Leonor’s headgear and robe are far more elaborate than her sister’s, as would have befitted the dowager queen of France. With their half-closed eyes and enveloping garments, they are as unobtrusive as their royal rank will permit and evidently related to each other.

Both Philip the Fair and Juana of Castile were regarded as attractive, but their children, especially Charles and Ferdinand, exhibited extreme versions of the Habsburgs’ hereditary long heads, short upper jaws, pendulous lower lip, and protruding mandible; Charles could not close his mouth (which led to the Elizabethan English jeer “jump as Germins’ lips,” in which “jump” meant “aligned”). Their mother’s alleged madness and their odd facial features—both Leonor and Mary are long of face and large of jaw, and Mary, at least, was accused of looking and acting mannish—had no effect on these siblings’ acuity, but their portraits turn that distinctive appearance into a mark of their well-attested personal distinction. The accomplishments of these two well-loved, highly competent women put them beyond conventional standards of beauty, though Mary, certainly, would have welcomed a life of less constant scrutiny, both public and familial.

Advertisement

It was Mary who acquired Hunt at the Castle of Torgau in Honor of Charles V (1544), a detail of which appears on the cover of the first volume of The Female Perspective. It is part of a marvelous series by Lucas Cranach the Elder depicting an imaginary hunting expedition in which Mary’s brother Charles chases down deer and wildfowl along the banks of a turbulent river that wends its roiling way beneath Torgau, the castle home of Elector Johann Friedrich of Saxony and his wife, Sibylle of Cleves. Sibylle had married Johann Friedrich in 1527, having narrowly avoided becoming the fourth wife of Henry VIII; the English king chose her sister Anne instead and then famously rejected her as unattractive. Cranach, always a great painter of women, took many an opportunity to portray Sibylle as a cat-eyed beauty of marked intelligence; here she leads the ladies of her court, all in expensive red livery, in pursuit of pheasant. The Electress of Saxony outdoes them all in a low-cut, daringly backless bodice (saved from scandal by a modest linen undershirt) above a pleated skirt of gold-embroidered velvet, ribbons twined around her silken sleeves, and three coral necklaces piled around her neck. Silk turban and rakishly angled velvet cap firmly in place, Sibylle looks coyly back over her shoulder as she aims a loaded crossbow with feline precision. Not surprisingly, this sixteenth-century pistolera was also an avid chess player, and Mary, an accomplished pistolera in her own right, must have seen in her a kindred soul.

Mary’s collection also contained Titian’s 1548 portrait of Sibylle’s husband after Charles V had defeated him in battle, a painful red sword slash disfiguring his portly face in a rare, raw picture of defeat. The paintings Mary commissioned from the Venetian master were similarly fierce images of punishment: large canvases showing the hellish agonies of the great mythological sinners Sisyphus, Tityus, Tantalus, and Ixion. The paintings of Tantalus and Ixion have disappeared, but Sisyphus, pushing his stone forever uphill, and Tityus, chain-bound with an eagle devouring his liver, still decorate the walls of the Prado. Miguel Falomir has written the entry on these images, noting that large male nudes in contorted positions are, to say the least, an unusual choice of subject for an aristocratic woman intent on commissioning mythological paintings for her castle, but the chatelaine of Binche was not an ordinary aristocratic woman; she was a head of state making an aggressive assertion of her authority. The magnificent equestrian portrait Titian painted of her brother Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg (in which Johann Friedrich of Saxony came to grief) somehow ended up in Mary’s collection, too.

The second volume of The Female Perspective introduces us to, among other characters, two of the figures in Las Meninas (1656), the monumental painting by Diego Velázquez that dominates one gallery of the Prado today: the tiny Infanta Margarita Teresa and her mother, Mariana of Austria, barely visible as a reflected image in a mirror alongside her husband, King Philip IV.

Both Mariana and her daughter, pawns in the Habsburg dynasty’s perpetual effort to retain control of both Spain and the Holy Roman Empire (i.e., Austria), were married off at fifteen to their respective uncles, Philip IV of Spain and Leopold I of Austria, in hopes of producing heirs of the most refined royal blood, a preoccupation further reinforced by the Spanish obsession, from the time of Isabella of Castile, with limpieza de sangre—the absence of non-Christian ancestry. Rather than purity, of course, that obsession brought on all the problems of inbreeding that contemporaries must have recognized from their experience with dogs and horses but failed to apply to the procreation of human beings. Mariana’s only surviving son, Charles II, was so visibly frail that she acted as his regent; her daughter, Margarita Teresa, worn out by the birth of four children (three of whom died as infants) and two miscarriages in the span of six years, died during her seventh pregnancy at the age of twenty-one.

The infanta’s legacy to the Prado consists mostly of the stream of portraits her formidable mother commissioned at every stage of the girl’s short life; she was identifiable from the age of three by the smooth shock of blonde hair that swept across her forehead from a side part and was secured by a barrette above the opposite ear. The part changed sides, but the hairdo was immutable, the essence of her identity among legions of long-faced Habsburg women. Most of her portraits were sent to Vienna as a reminder of her eligibility as a potential consort to her uncle Leopold, but some remained in Spain to reinforce the image of an attractive young woman with a pronounced talent for music.

Mariana, on the other hand, was a force to be reckoned with from the day she arrived in Madrid as a teenager. Las Meninas may portray her through a glass, darkly, but Velázquez also painted the queen consort around 1665 in full regalia, immobilized beneath a broad beribboned wig and a hoop-skirted gown so wide that she cannot bring her arms down to her sides. The face that looks out from under all the finery is alert, wary, and acutely human. A scarlet satin drape has been drawn aside to unveil her like a mystery or a dramatic spectacle, while in the background stands, in splendid isolation, a mechanical clock. Mariana was a woman who knew how to bide her time. Her marriage to Philip, despite the thirty-year difference in their ages, lasted nearly a quarter-century, and it was Philip who secured her right to act as regent for their three-year-old son, Charles II, much against the wishes of other figures at court.

As a widow, Mariana exchanged her wigs and farthingales for a nunlike ensemble of white robe and black veil and ruled on her son’s behalf for ten years. A portrait from circa 1670 by Velázquez’s student Juan Carreño de Miranda shows how cleverly she uses the royal art collections to advance her claims to rule and the price of defiance: Jacopo Tintoretto’s Judith and Holofernes (1577), with its implicit threat—“Mess with me and I’ll have your head”—hangs in the Prado next to Titian’s cringeworthy Philip II Offering the Infante Fernando to Victory (1573–1575), almost certainly the product of the great Venetian’s workshop rather than his own, by then arthritic, hands. A palace revolt displaced Mariana and the infante from Madrid for two years, but in 1679 Charles returned at eighteen to assume the kingship until his death in 1700, and Mariana, until her own death in 1696, remained a power behind the throne.

Characteristically she chose to mark her return with an auto-da-fé in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor in 1680. Francisco Rizi’s painting of the event, completed in 1683, now hangs in the Prado, a grim reminder of Mariana’s noted “Austrian” piety. Seated next to her son and his consort, Marie-Louise of Orléans, she holds a prayer book as the Inquisition immolates heretics. It was also she, apparently, who decided that lying in a coffin next to the exhumed remains of her late husband would help poor Charles to conceive a child, despite his physical inability to do so. (His autopsy revealed a single shriveled testicle.)

It is a great relief to move from the Dowager Queen Mariana to an older contemporary who flatly refused to become the mother of kings: Christina of Sweden, who converted to Catholicism in Lutheran Uppsala, abdicated, and moved to Italy with the hope of becoming queen of Naples. To that end she sent a series of paintings and sculptures to Philip IV that now grace the Prado: an equestrian portrait by Sebastien Bourdon keeps comparatively modest company with Titian’s splendid equestrian image of Charles V, Velázquez’s equestrian portrait of the Count-Duke Olivares, and an Adam and Eve by Albrecht Dürer.

The most impressive legacy to the Prado, however, came a generation later, through the offices of another consort from another dynasty: Isabella Farnese, the sole, and fascinating, protagonist of The Female Perspective’s third volume. Isabella was the second wife of Philip V, crowned king of Spain in 1700 after Charles II named him as his successor in his will. The Bourbon prince—the grandson of Louis XIV and his Spanish wife, Maria Teresa, the daughter of Philip IV—had an excellent claim to the vacant throne. The seventeen-year-old Philip V then faced another fourteen years of bitter warfare as the Sun King and the Habsburgs of Austria, who also claimed the Kingdom of Spain, fought the War of the Spanish Succession; Philip finally retained his crown by renouncing any right to rule France. His first wife, the popular Maria Luisa Gabriella of Savoy, died in February 1714, a month before the war ended. A search went out immediately for a new consort.

It was this fraught political situation and the vast expenses incurred by years of war that turned the daughter of a provincial grand duke into a possible candidate for the next royal alliance. As the sole heiress to the family of the Dukes of Parma and Piacenza, Isabella Farnese was, as Jane Austen might say, possessed of a large fortune. Smallpox had left her face slightly scarred (but also eliminated the threat of that deadly disease), and at eighteen she was healthy and energetic, in contrast to the frail Maria Luisa. Furthermore, as the heiress to a minor if prosperous Italian state, with a pope in her lineage and a Habsburg connection (her great-great-grandfather Ottavio was married to Margaret of Parma, known as “Madama,” the spirited illegitimate daughter of Charles V), the grandees of the Spanish court would have regarded her as respectable but definitely of lower rank than themselves, and thus someone who could be held in check without much difficulty. The influential Cardinal Giulio Alberoni, a longtime agent for the Farnese family, reported that she was an obedient girl of limited intelligence.

The Farnese family’s view of itself was rather different. The fifteenth-century chronicler Annius of Viterbo traced their lineage back to the Etruscans and ancient Egypt, and they continued to boast of that Etruscan identity long after Annius had been exposed as a forger. As far as the Farnese were concerned, they had been civilized long before the Romans conquered the barbarian tribesmen of the Iberian peninsula. Local archives in their ancestral haunts just north of Rome recorded the family’s presence since the tenth century. They could boast only one pope, Paul III, but he had strutted across the same historical stage as Charles V and rubbed elbows with Titian and Michelangelo. The Farnese built palazzi as big as their own self-image and amassed collections of art and antiquities extensive enough to fill them. Four generations after Ottavio Farnese and his Habsburg wife went off to make their home in Parma, something of Madama’s brio was still detectable in the Archduchess Isabella.

Isabella Farnese married Philip V by proxy in 1714 before undertaking a long, unhurried journey overland to Madrid. For a full three weeks she stopped in Pau, at the foot of the Pyrenees just short of the Spanish border, where Cardinal Alberoni instructed her in the ways of the Spanish court. Above all he warned her about Marie-Anne de la Trémoille, Princesse des Ursins, the late queen’s camarera mayor de palacio (chief lady-in-waiting) and reputedly the chief power behind the throne. The Princesse had hoped at first to succeed her mistress as queen; when that outcome looked impossible, she encouraged the choice of Isabella, sure that the young woman would prove as malleable as the thirteen-year-old Maria Luisa had proven in her day. When the two finally met, the Princesse lost no time in asserting her fearsome authority. “You’re late,” she scolded. (The queen had taken three months to join her husband.) “You’re banished,” Isabella replied. The Princesse protested. The king backed his wife. His support for his queen never wavered. Indeed, he took up residence in her apartments for the rest of his life.

Philip had always been subject to bouts of melancholy; fourteen years on a wobbly throne amid a raging war might erode a person’s confidence. Isabella eventually hired the famous Italian castrato Farinelli to sing to him as a form of music therapy, and she quickly learned to take over whenever he felt out of sorts, which was much of the time. She bore him seven children in addition to the four he had already sired with Maria Luisa, including the two sons who came before her own firstborn, Charles, in the line of succession. The first of these princely heirs, Louis, was crowned king in 1724 when Philip briefly abdicated but died seven months later. The second, Ferdinand, ascended to the throne when Philip died in 1746 and spent the next thirteen years in constant conflict with his potent stepmother.

Isabella’s son Charles, in the meantime, had secured the Spanish hold on Italy, reigning as Duke of Parma and Piacenza from 1731 and as king of Naples and Sicily from 1735. A great patron of art in his own right, he began the excavations at Pompeii (1748) and Herculaneum (1738) and in 1731 he initiated the transfer of the immense Farnese collection of antique statues to Naples from Rome (a process completed by his son and successor, Ferdinand IV). In 1759 Charles was finally crowned king of Spain, with his mother acting as regent for the three months it took to tear him away from Naples and pack him off to Spain in October of the same year. The dowager queen died in 1766 at the age of seventy-three.

With “The Female Perspective,” the Prado is rewriting the history of this enterprising woman who purchased a thousand paintings for the royal collection, marking them as hers with a discreet white stylized lily in the corner—not a French royal fleur-de-lis (although that was also hers by right of marriage) but a Farnese giglio. Three hundred and fifty-eight paintings and a large number of sculptures make up her contribution to the Prado’s collection and to “The Female Perspective.” The volume dedicated to this strong-willed, fearless queen emphasizes all the ways in which she used works of art to enhance her claims to her throne and to create an image of herself for the Spanish public. Noelia García Pérez’s opening essay provides a trenchant contrast to the account of the queen that we find in the authoritative Treccani Dictionary of Italian Biography, an entry written, moreover, by a woman scholar:

As for the young Isabella Farnese’s education, we know nothing definite; the later letters of her stepfather to Cardinal Alberoni enumerate her great intellectual gifts: she was taught to read and write in Latin, French, and German, and to dedicate hours of study to books on religion and history. But one has the impression that the portrait has been overdrawn and that the pitiless, albeit biased, image of her that emerges from the pages of Saint-Simon may be somewhat more accurate: a mediocre, if notably sly, intelligence, the lack of any real intellectual tastes, the absence of any capacity to acquire them in the face of a temperament as wilful as that wilfulness was well concealed.

García Pérez seems to be writing about an entirely different person:

During her stay in the principality of Monaco, she made a profound impression on Antonio I Grimaldi, who wrote a description of the young princess that was both accurate and revealing…. What most caught the prince’s attention was the natural grace of her presence, with a friendly smile, charming voice, and the use of the most exquisitely courteous phrases. Grimaldi saw something unusual in the queen for a young woman of her age: a resolute will and calm confidence that did not require gestures to be imposed. He also astutely noted that “due to her character, one would take her for a Florentine.” He concluded his description by emphasizing that Isabella possessed a great heart and that what above all distinguished her from other princesses was the attitude with which she faced the world.

At the Prado, we can see how she presented herself in her 1739 state portrait by Louis-Michel van Loo: clad in golden brocade, ermine tails dripping from her bodice and the lining of her mantle, a pearl bracelet with a cameo portrait of her husband on her left wrist, and her right hand pointing to her crown resting temporarily on a red velvet pillow. Her scarlet mantle and the throne behind her are embroidered in gold with lions, castles, and fleurs-de-lis—French, of course, but also Farnese. Her hair is fashionably powdered, her aspect that of a mature woman, and distinctly maternal. After more than a decade of marriage, her position as the mother of her family and her adopted nation are beyond dispute.

Without Isabella Farnese the Prado would have no paintings by Bartolomé Esteban Murillo, the seventeenth-century artist whose sensitive images of the Madonna and Child rank among its most beloved works. It is she who sought out and snapped up the portrait Diego Velázquez painted of his wife, Juana Pacheco, as a Sibyl, two country scenes by Watteau, a John the Baptist inspired by Caravaggio and painted by the eighteenth-century Neapolitan master Francesco Solimena, a full complement of works by Rubens and Van Dyck, and rarities by masters she knew from the Farnese family collections that are now housed in Naples: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Correggio, Parmigianino. It was she who wrested Queen Christina of Sweden’s collection of antique statues in Rome from their last heir, Baldassarre Odescalchi, obtained a papal waiver to take them out of the Papal States, and arranged their shipment from the Roman port of Ripa Grande to Civitavecchia, across the sea to Alicante, and onward, via “covered waggons pulled by oxen,” to Segovia.

The hunt for the treasures she bequeathed to the Prado takes visitors all over the museum, and not surprisingly it was her son, Charles III, who commissioned the building itself in 1785, to house a new royal museum of natural history. Between them they were instrumental in bringing the eighteenth-century Enlightenment to both Naples and Madrid, inspired, in stark contrast to the last Habsburg rulers, by a passionate vision of a more universal idea of the common good and public service.

A similar vision stands behind the successive installments of “The Female Perspective” at the Prado. By seeing the women who contributed to its history as more complete characters, we also see their contemporaries, both female and male, in greater depth. (The sympathetic presentation of the hapless Charles II in Volume II is one example, emphasizing his human dignity rather than his physical defects—there was a sensitive person inside that beleaguered body and ungainly face.) The Female Perspective is really a universal perspective, just as Spain’s national collection really belongs to all of humanity. .
